strengths: The flat map tokenization is a clean, well-motivated middle ground between lossy parcellation and expensive native 4D volumetric tokenization: it preserves full cortical signal, injects a spatial locality inductive bias, and lets the paper reuse standard ViT/MAE machinery (plus a simple, well-justified modification for ~40% background pixels).

The scaling study over pretraining dataset sizes (0.5M to 7.4M frames, 59–979 subjects) is a genuinely useful observation: strict power-law scaling of in-distribution reconstruction loss, with an honest demonstration that OOD (NSD) scaling saturates and that downstream decoding does NOT scale monotonically — the paper correctly interprets this as a data-diversity issue rather than overclaiming.

Downstream results are strong where comparable: 98.8% on HCP 21-class state decoding (well above the patch-embedding baseline at 94.1% and prior reported ~93-95%), and 84.6% on UKBB sex classification despite training only a frozen-encoder attentive probe on 16s clips and cross-dataset transfer (HCP→UKBB), vs. prior work that pretrains and fine-tunes on UKBB with >320s sequences.

Good open-science posture: public HCP/NSD/UKBB data, released code and flat-map datasets, an explicit 'work in progress' framing with an open project and honest discussion of limitations (non-monotonic downstream scaling, HCP diversity, difficulty of cross-paper benchmark comparison).
Pretraining implementation details are unusually thorough for the scale (625K steps, AdamW settings, repeated sampling, ~27 H100-hours per ViT-B run), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central comparative claim (flat maps are a good tokenization for fMRI foundation models) is not tested against the approaches it positions itself between. There is no parcellation-based MAE baseline, no volume-based baseline (e.g., BrainLM, SWIFT, Brain-JEPA, NeuroSTORM retrained under matched conditions), and no fine-tuning experiments — only frozen-encoder probes against two weak baselines (connectome, patch embedding). The paper itself lists direct comparisons as 'active research directions,' which is honest but means the core methodological claim rests on indirect evidence.

The 'strict power law' scaling claim is fit from only 5 dataset-size points, with model size and compute fixed (so it is a data-scaling law only, not a Kaplan/Charging-style study), and no seed variance is reported anywhere; single-seed differences of ~0.3-1% in Figure 4 are interpreted without uncertainty estimates.

The scaling law holds only for reconstruction loss; the downstream story is explicitly non-monotonic (3.2M frames beats 7.4M on both OOD benchmarks, and the largest model ViT-L underperforms), which weakens the 'hallmark of an effective foundation model' framing in the abstract and introduction.

The 98.8% HCP state decoding result 'approaching ceiling' deserves more scrutiny: task-evoked decoding at this accuracy can reflect shared stimulus/task timing structure, and the paper does not analyze whether the probe exploits stimulus-locked temporal structure (e.g., via the pt=2 ablation gain) or genuine distributed representations; no confusion analysis or per-class breakdown is provided.

The NSD CLIP benchmark is self-constructed with noisy pseudo-labels (CLIP nearest-neighbor over 41 manually curated captions, acknowledged as 'ambiguous, ill-posed'), making the 20.6% accuracy hard to interpret without a human-vision or stimulus-information ceiling estimate.

No limitations section in the main text proper; limitations are distributed through the narrative and conclusion. Minor: the flat map projection involves relaxation cuts and arbitrary 2D parameterization choices (grid fit, 1.2mm resolution) whose sensitivity is not ablated.

strengths: The flat map tokenization is a sensible middle ground between lossy parcellation and expensive native 4D tokenization, and is well motivated (preserves full cortical signal while injecting locality inductive biases and enabling standard ViT tooling).

The scaling analysis on masked reconstruction is the clearest result: in-distribution reconstruction loss follows a clean power law across four dataset sizes, which the authors correctly highlight as a first for fMRI foundation models.

Downstream results are genuinely promising in places: 98.8% on HCP 21-class state decoding (well above their own patch-embedding baseline at 94.1% and reported prior work), and near-SOTA UKBB sex classification (84.6% vs. Brain-JEPA's 88.6%) despite pretraining on a different dataset with a frozen encoder and short 16s clips.

The paper is honest about its preliminary status, openly discusses OOD saturation and non-monotonic downstream scaling, and provides substantial methodological detail (flat map construction, preprocessing, probe protocols, new NSD benchmark construction) supporting reproducibility; code and data are stated to be released.
The observation that small models (12.4M params) nearly match ViT-B, and that smaller temporal patches help across all benchmarks, are useful practical findings for the community.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly framed as 'a work in progress' / preliminary evaluation, which is better suited to a workshop, preprint, or open-science venue than the ICML main track; the contributions (apply VideoMAE to flat maps; measure a scaling curve) are incremental applications of existing methods (MAE/VideoMAE, standard ViT) to a new data modality.

The headline 'scaling law' claim is only supported for the in-distribution reconstruction loss on four data points; OOD reconstruction (Figure 3b) visibly deviates from the power law, and downstream decoding shows weak, non-monotonic dataset-size effects (the largest model is best only on HCP; the 3.2M-frame model wins on both OOD benchmarks). Thus the central promise of the paper—scaling data improves fMRI representations—is not demonstrated for the representations that matter.

Baselines are thin: no direct comparison against alternative tokenizations under the same MAE recipe (e.g., parcellation tokens or native 4D with the same compute budget), so the core claim that flat maps are the right representation is not isolated from the benefit of MAE pretraining itself. The simple patch-embedding baseline nearly matches the pretrained model on UKBB (76.6% vs. 84.6% is the gap, but on HCP the gap analysis is confounded by different protocol), and the connectome baseline remains competitive on some tasks.

Several key results lack statistical treatment: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests for downstream accuracies; differences between configurations (e.g., 2.2M vs. 12.4M vs. 86M models; dataset-size subsets) can be within noise, making conclusions like 'small models are sufficient' or the ViT-L 'notably worse' anomaly hard to trust.

The new NSD CLIP classification benchmark is acknowledged by the authors as 'ambiguous, ill-posed' (CLIP-assigned global labels from 41 captions), which weakens it as evidence; its main purpose appears to be having a benchmark where the model wins by a large margin.

The claimed general-purpose cross-subject visual decoding step is modest in absolute terms (NSD CLIP accuracy only ~4% above held-out training-subject gap is not clearly quantified), and clinical translatability motivates the introduction but is never evaluated.

Comparison to prior work is complicated by differing splits/protocols, which the authors themselves admit, so 'approaching SOTA' claims on UKBB and 'matching' prior methods on HCP are not apples-to-apples.

strengths: The flat map tokenization is a well-motivated intermediate representation between lossy parcellation and expensive native 4D modeling: it preserves full cortical signal while injecting a locality inductive bias and enabling standard ViT/MAE machinery with only a minor modification (background-pixel masking).

The dataset-size scaling experiment (Figure 3a) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding: a clean power-law fit for in-distribution masked reconstruction across 0.5M–7.4M frames is, as the authors note, a first for fMRI foundation modeling, and the observed saturation for OOD (NSD) data is reported honestly rather than hidden.

Downstream results are promising: 98.8% on HCP 21-class state decoding exceeds best reported numbers in comparable setups, and cross-dataset transfer to UKBB and NSD (frozen encoder, zero-shot on an unseen subject for NSD) is a meaningful demonstration.

Evaluation design is careful: frozen-encoder attentive probes applied uniformly across fm-MAE and baselines, family-aware subject splits, hyperparameter sweeps on validation only, and clear reporting of confounds in cross-paper comparisons (splits, sequence lengths, fine-tuning).
Strong reproducibility: full implementation details (optimizers, schedules, compute cost, flat-map construction) plus released code and data, and an explicitly open, collaborative framing.
weaknesses: The headline scaling-law claim is weaker than the framing suggests. The power law holds only for in-distribution reconstruction loss with a single model size (ViT-B) over a limited data range; downstream decoding shows a weak, non-monotonic dataset-size effect, and OOD reconstruction saturates. The paper acknowledges this, but the abstract and intro lead with the scaling result while the more decision-relevant evidence (representations) does not scale cleanly.

There are no direct comparisons to existing fMRI foundation models (BrainLM, Brain-JEPA, SWIFT, NeuroSTORM, BrainNetwork Transformer) under a shared protocol. The baseline set (connectome features and a patch-embedding probe) is minimal, so the central claim that flat maps are a better tokenization than alternatives is not established head-to-head. The authors list this as future work, but for an ICML submission this is a significant gap.

The patch-embedding baseline already achieves 94.1% on HCP state decoding — matching prior SOTA — which raises the question of how much of the reported downstream strength comes from the flat-map representation plus attentive probe rather than from the MAE pretraining itself; an ablation disentangling pretraining from architecture/probe choice is missing.

Cross-paper comparisons (98.8% vs. 94.8% vs. 93.4%) are confounded by differing splits, clip lengths, and evaluation protocols; the authors are transparent about this, but it means the SOTA-level claim cannot be taken at face value.

The NSD CLIP benchmark is newly constructed by the authors (CLIP-assigned labels, 41 categories) with no external validation, and the achieved ~21% accuracy, while >8x chance, is low in absolute terms; the 'signs of life' framing is honest but the significance of this result is hard to judge.

The paper is explicitly a work-in-progress ('ongoing open project'); several directions a mature contribution would include — diverse pretraining data, alternative SSL objectives, direct baselines, representation analysis — are deferred. This limits the contribution's finality for a main-track publication.

No discussion of limitations or ethics as a dedicated section: sex classification and stated clinical motivations ('unlock novel clinical applications') carry well-known risks (biomarker misuse, generalization failures across populations, demographic confounds in UKBB) that go unaddressed.

Flat-map projection involves interpolation and relaxation cuts (Figure 6) that distort the cortical sheet; the claim of preserving 'full dimensionality' glosses over information loss and geometric distortion introduced by flattening, which is not quantified.

strengths: The flat map representation is a simple but genuinely novel input formulation for fMRI foundation models, and the paper tests it rigorously: all three representations (parcel, flat map, volume) are trained with matched architectures, matched patch sequence lengths, and 8 pretraining seeds, making the representation comparison unusually controlled for this field.

BRAINMARKS addresses a real, documented problem (irreproducible fMRI evaluation) with an open, unified benchmark covering 6 prior foundation models plus an FC baseline, spanning both trait prediction and dynamic state decoding — a substantial community resource.

The paper is exceptionally honest: it reports a null result on trait prediction (no model beats a functional connectivity baseline), documents where its own representation loses (volume best on age; parcel most efficient), notes the exponent of its scaling law is -0.01 vs -0.1 in language modeling, and acknowledges tension between Figure 11 and Figure 7c.

Reproducibility is strong: open code, models, and data; detailed hyperparameters (Table 7-8), preprocessing pipelines, probe protocols, compute accounting (~7K H100 hours), and a careful cross-model comparison protocol including the coordinate normalization analysis (Tables 6, 15) that explains prior models' apparent failures fairly.

The scaling analysis (Figures 7a-d) with downstream accuracy scaling is the first of its kind for fMRI, and the OOD degradation findings (NSD vs HCP-YA, UKBB underperforming HCP-YA despite 10x more data) are informative negative/nuanced results.

Extensive, well-organized ablations (masking, augmentation, reconstruction targets, temporal patch size, subcortical inclusion, normalization, decoder architecture) that largely explain design choices and identify open problems (data augmentation, fine-grained targets).
weaknesses: The core method is a direct adaptation of MAE-st to a new data modality; the scientific novelty rests primarily on the input representation choice and the empirical study rather than methodological innovation, which some readers may find incremental.

The scaling-law claim ('strict power law') is fitted from only the three smallest data splits per the figure caption, and the very small exponent plus saturation at 37M parameters weakens the claim; the paper itself hedges ('albeit with limits').

Benchmark fairness concerns: CortexMAE and Brain-Semantoks are the only models with multi-seed confidence intervals, and the finding that several baselines were 'pretrained without coordinate normalization' means the headline SotA result partly reflects preprocessing compatibility with the benchmark protocol rather than pure representation quality; the paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve this (no model-specific nuisance regression strategies).

The flat map representation excludes subcortical structures by construction; the mitigation (Table 5 showing subcortical inclusion does not help) relies only on parcellation-based models, so the impact on dense representations remains untested.

State decoding benchmarks are in-distribution-flavored for HCP-YA pretraining (Task21 covers the same cognitive tasks seen during pretraining), which the paper notes but which tempers the generality of the SotA claim; the NSD COCO24 setup with 4s trials and 16s clips is a non-standard decoding task whose construct validity could be debated.

Clinical/trait datasets are small (400-900 subjects) with high class imbalance, so the negative trait-prediction result, while honestly reported, may partly reflect statistical power rather than a fundamental limitation of foundation models.

strengths: The paper is a careful, systematic empirical study of a genuinely important question for fMRI modeling: how should fMRI data be represented for self-supervised learning? The direct comparison of parcellation, flat map, and volume representations within a single controlled model family (same architecture, compute budget, pretraining data) is a real contribution that prior work has not provided.

Reproducibility and evaluation rigor are exceptional for this subfield: 8 pretraining repeats with random seeds, ±std reporting, 3σ significance thresholds for claims of robust differences, a unified probe-based evaluation protocol applied uniformly to 6 prior foundation models, and full release of code, models, and data. The BRAINMARKS suite itself is a significant community contribution addressing a documented reproducibility gap.

The paper is unusually honest: it reports a challenging null result (no model reliably beats a functional-connectivity baseline on trait prediction), documents that prior models were likely handicapped by missing coordinate normalization (and quantifies this in Tables 6 and 15), and openly discusses tensions between results (e.g., Figure 11 vs. Figure 7c) and limitations (cortex-only representation, single-dataset pretraining, weaker scaling exponent of -0.01).

The ablation studies are thorough and informative (masking, augmentation, reconstruction targets, temporal/spatial patch size, input normalization, data mixture, cross-register decoding), and several findings (emergent default-mode structure in position embeddings, decoder edge masking to prevent interpolation shortcuts) are of independent interest.

The scaling analysis (Figure 7) is the first of its kind for fMRI and is presented with appropriate caveats about saturation and weak OOD generalization, which usefully tempers 'bigger is better' assumptions in this domain.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the core contribution is applying the existing MAE-st recipe to flat maps produced by an existing tool (pycortex). The 'goldilocks zone' hypothesis is a framing rather than a validated theory, and the evidence is mixed by the authors' own admission (flat maps do not uniformly win; volume wins on age prediction, parcel is most efficient).

The flat map representation's advantage is confined to state decoding; on the more clinically motivated trait prediction benchmarks the paper reports essentially no reliable advantage for any foundation model over simple baselines. This substantially narrows the demonstrated practical payoff of the proposed representation.

The CortexMAE-V advantage on HCP-A age (and to a degree the cross-model comparisons) is complicated by preprocessing asymmetries: HCP-A uses ICA-FIX denoising while HCP-YA does not, and the authors do not implement model-specific nuisance regression, so the fairness of the cross-model trait prediction comparison remains imperfectly resolved.

The cortex-only flat map excludes subcortical structures, and the authors' mitigation (Table 5) only tests the parcellation variant, not whether a cortex+subcortical dense representation would change conclusions. Applicability to clinical datasets with atypical anatomy or non-standard preprocessing (common in ADNI/ABIDE-type data) is not directly evaluated.

All pretraining is from a single dataset (HCP-YA, young adults), and the UKBB comparison in Figure 11 is acknowledged as preliminary with a much less tested pipeline, so claims about dataset choice remain provisional.

The scaling 'laws' have a very weak exponent (-0.01 vs -0.1 in language modeling) and saturate at small model sizes, so the scaling framing in the title oversells what is actually a modest, saturating trend; 'strict power law scaling' with such an exponent is of limited practical guidance.

strengths: Technically solid and unusually thorough empirical work: the CortexMAE family is trained with 8 pretraining repeats across representations, enabling robust statistical comparisons (Table 2), and the paper reports null results (trait prediction) honestly rather than overclaiming.

Flat map representation is a simple but genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution: it preserves full cortical signal, reduces dimensionality, injects geometric inductive bias, and is directly compatible with standard ViT/MAE-st, sidestepping heavy architecture engineering.

BRAINMARKS is a significant community contribution: the first open, reproducible evaluation suite for fMRI foundation models spanning trait and state prediction, with a carefully controlled probe protocol (logistic probes with 100 randomized splits for small-sample trait tasks; attentive probes with dense LR grids for state tasks) applied uniformly to 6 prior models.

The scaling analysis (Figure 7) is the first systematic one for fMRI, and the paper is candid about its limits (weak exponent of -0.01, saturation at ~37M params, weak OOD transfer to NSD) rather than selling 'scaling laws' as an unqualified success.

Extensive ablations and supplementary analyses (masking, augmentation, temporal/spatial patch size, subcortex, normalization, data mixture, UKBB pretraining, decoder variants) provide real scientific insight, e.g., the finding that coordinate normalization is essential for state decoding (Table 6) and that structure emerges naturally in position embeddings (Figure 5).

Highly reproducible and open: code, models, datasets released; detailed hyperparameters and compute costs (~7K H100 hours) reported; explicit limitations and impact statement addressing ethical concerns about mental state decoding.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is a straightforward adaptation of existing techniques (MAE-st applied to pycortex flat maps); the novelty rests mainly on the representation choice and the systematic evaluation rather than new modeling ideas.

Pretraining is limited to a single, demographically homogeneous dataset (HCP-YA, ages 22-35); the acknowledged weak OOD generalization (NSD scaling slowdown, UKBB underperforming HCP-YA despite 10x more data, Figure 11) raises questions about the generality of the 'goldilocks zone' hypothesis beyond this regime.

The flat map representation excludes subcortical structures and depends on surface-based preprocessing pipelines, which may limit adoption; the subcortex ablation (Table 5) only tests this within the parcellation family, not for flat maps directly.

Cross-model benchmark comparisons are partially confounded by preprocessing differences: some prior models were pretrained without coordinate normalization, which the authors show drives near-chance state decoding (Tables 6, 15). The authors analyze this carefully, but the claimed SotA margin over prior work should be interpreted with this caveat.

Trait prediction null results, while honestly reported and scientifically valuable, mean the paper offers limited path toward the clinical applications motivating the introduction; the significance of the state-decoding gains rests on two benchmarks, one of which (Task21) is in-distribution with the pretraining tasks.

Some scaling evidence is internally in tension (Figure 11 continued-pretraining results vs Figure 7c), and the power-law fits are estimated from only the three smallest models/data splits, which weakens the 'strict power law' framing slightly.
